```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 5.5,
  dpi = 110,
  out.width = "100%"
)
library(sbert)
```

The `covid` dataset that ships with **sbert** holds 4,170 records of research
on COVID-19 and education, children, schools, and society, published from
2020 to 2024. This article finds the main themes in their abstracts.

**sbert** groups texts by what they mean. Each text becomes an embedding, a
vector of numbers in which texts with similar meaning lie close together, and
a topic is a group of texts whose embeddings are close. So we read each
topic's example texts first and use words only as labels at the end.

Abstracts are long. The default model reads at most 256 tokens of a text and
ignores the rest, and many abstracts are longer than that. So we fit topics
twice: once on whole abstracts, and once on their sentences, which are short
enough to be read in full. The two give different answers to different
questions.

Unlike the vignette, this article downloads a model and encodes about 3,800
abstracts and all their sentences. It takes a few minutes.

# Preparing the abstracts

`r nrow(subset(covid, Abstract == "[No abstract available]"))` records have no abstract,
only the placeholder `"[No abstract available]"`. We drop them.

```{r data}
abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")
nrow(abstracts)
```

Almost every abstract ends with a copyright notice, such as "© 2021 Informa UK
Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group." Left in, the notices would form
topics of their own, grouped by publisher rather than by research. The
`remove` argument of `clean_corpus()` deletes text that matches a regular
expression. The pattern below deletes a notice at the end of an abstract
that starts with "©", "Copyright ©", or "Copyright" and a year. It does not
touch abstracts that mention copyright as a subject.

`clean_corpus()` also repairs broken characters, removes HTML tags, URLs,
DOIs, and bracketed citations, and with `min_content = 0.5` drops rows that
are mostly numbers or symbols rather than words. Given a data frame and a
`column`, it cleans that column and keeps the other columns.

```{r clean}
abstracts <- clean_corpus(
  abstracts,
  column = "Abstract",
  remove = "(copyright:?\\s*(©|\\d{4})|©).{0,1000}$",
  min_content = 0.5
)
nrow(abstracts)
```

# The model

Install the ONNX Runtime and download the default model, `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`.
Both steps happen once per computer.

```{r runtime}
install_runtime()
model_download()
```

# Choosing the number of topics

`compare_topics()` fits one model for each topic count, here on both whole
abstracts (`"document"`) and sentences (`"sentence"`). `max_tokens = 200`
splits the rare sentence longer than 200 words at its punctuation, so that no
sentence is cut off.

Words such as *covid*, *pandemic*, and *study* appear in nearly every
abstract, so they are added to the standard English stop words, and
`numbers = "remove"` leaves out bare numbers such as years. Stop words affect
only the word labels and the word-based measures. The topics themselves are
computed from the embeddings of the full text.

```{r sweep}
covid_stop_words <- stop_words(add = c(
  "covid", "coronavirus", "sars", "cov", "pandemic", "disease",
  "study", "studies", "result", "results", "conclusion", "conclusions",
  "background", "method", "methods", "objective", "aim"
))

sweep <- compare_topics(
  abstracts,
  column = "Abstract",
  n_topics = c(4, 6, 8, 10, 12),
  segment = c("document", "sentence"),
  max_tokens = 200,
  stop_words = covid_stop_words,
  numbers = "remove"
)
sweep
```

```{r sweep-plot, fig.height=4.5}
plot(sweep)
```

On whole abstracts, coherence jumps from 0.07 at six topics to 0.18 at
eight. The jump is not what it seems. From eight topics on, one topic holds
only three abstracts that are not about education at all, and their rare
words (*ECMO*, *porcine*, *polymers*) always occur together, so that topic
alone has a coherence of 0.90 and lifts the mean. The other seven topics
average 0.08, only a little above six topics. We still use eight: the topics
are a little more coherent and more diverse than at six, and the small topic
is useful because it isolates papers that do not belong in this corpus.

On sentences, coherence changes little from one count to the next. We use
eight there too, so that the two models can be compared.

```{r model}
topic_model <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 8, segment = "document")
```

# What the abstracts are about

`representatives()` returns, for each topic, the abstracts closest to that
topic and clearly farther from every other topic. Here is one per topic, in
full:

```{r representatives}
knitr::kable(representatives(topic_model, n = 1), digits = 2)
```

The plot shows the opening of three abstracts per topic:

```{r plot-representatives, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 12}
plot(topic_model, type = "representatives", n_representatives = 3)
```

Read together, the examples show eight subjects:

1. Students' acceptance of and satisfaction with online learning, mostly
   surveys.
2. Teachers and emergency remote teaching in schools.
3. Laboratory and hands-on courses moved online, in engineering and
   chemistry.
4. Social and political commentary: images on social media, grassroots
   organizing, community solidarity.
5. Surgical and medical training.
6. Universities as institutions: their finances, international students,
   and private higher education.
7. Young children, parents, and families during school and daycare closures.
8. Three papers outside education: a training model for ECMO, marine
   plastic litter, and anatomy teaching by dissection.

`topic_sizes()` counts the abstracts in each topic. The first three topics,
on online learning, teachers, and laboratory courses, hold more than half of
them.

```{r sizes}
topic_sizes(topic_model)
```

# What the sentences are about

The sentence model was fitted in the same call. `fitted()` returns it. Its
example sentences are short enough to read in full:

```{r sentence-model}
sentence_model <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 8, segment = "sentence")
knitr::kable(representatives(sentence_model, n = 3), digits = 2)
```

Most sentence topics are not subjects but the jobs that sentences do in an
abstract:

- Topic 1 opens an abstract by saying what the pandemic did to education.
- Topic 5 holds general, hedging sentences ("However, the processes involved
  in making this happen are elusive and complex.").
- Topic 6 reports samples and response rates ("Of 268 students enrolled, 104
  responded").
- Topic 7 describes methods of data collection and analysis.
- Topic 8 states the pandemic as background ("The WHO has stated the
  outbreak of COVID-19 as a pandemic issue.").

Only three are subjects: perceptions of online education (topic 2), course
design with labs, simulations, and hybrid teaching (topic 3), and education
policy and inequality (topic 4).

`topic_sizes(by = "document")` counts how many abstracts have at least one
sentence in each topic:

```{r sentence-sizes}
topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document")
```

`topic_gamma()` gives the mix of topics in each abstract: the share of its
sentences that fall in each topic. The shares of an abstract add up to 1.

```{r gamma}
head(topic_gamma(sentence_model), 16)
```

# The words each topic uses

`summary()` lists each topic under its label, the opening of its most
central abstract or sentence, and reports the coherence of its top words.
`terms()` lists those words.

```{r summary}
summary(topic_model)
```

```{r terms}
terms(topic_model, n = 5)
```

The words say much less than the examples. Topics 1 and 3 have almost the
same top words (*online*, *learning*, *students*), yet one is about
students' acceptance of online learning and the other about laboratory
courses moved online. Words such as *learning*, *students*, and *online* run
through the whole corpus, so they cannot tell these topics apart. The
embeddings can, because they capture what each abstract says rather than
which words it uses.

The sentence topics' words are vaguer still. Only topic 7's top words,
*data*, *analysis*, and *used*, are clear, because sentences about methods
reuse the same few words. None of the words shows what most sentence topics
do: open an abstract, report a sample, or hedge.

```{r sentence-summary}
summary(sentence_model)
```

# Which model to use

The two models answer different questions. Whole abstracts group papers by
subject: who was studied and what was taught. Sentences group mainly by what
a sentence does in an abstract (context, sample, method, hedging), with a few
subject topics among them. Almost every abstract (79%) has a sentence in
topic 1, the opening context.

Use whole abstracts to map the research themes of a literature. Use
sentences to study how abstracts are written, or to reach content beyond the
first 256 tokens of long abstracts, which the whole-abstract model never
reads.

# Next steps

- `predict(topic_model, new_abstracts)` assigns new abstracts to these topics
  without refitting. For the sentence model it splits the new abstracts into
  sentences in the same way.
- `reduce_topics(topic_model, n_topics = 4)` merges similar topics, and
  `topic_hierarchy()` shows which topics are closest to each other.
- The article *Parallel and High-Throughput Topic Modeling* shows how to
  encode once and reuse the embeddings across many fits and sessions.
